articles.headline: GM to pay $220 million after selling customer Smart Driver data
keyFacts: General Motors will pay $220 million to settle lawsuits with the District of Columbia and 35 states over selling customer driving data to insurance companies.
Attorneys general sued GM after discovering that the automaker shared Smart Driver data with brokers without proper customer consent.
Under the settlement, a third party will be required to ensure GM complies with its privacy policy.
body: General Motors marketed its Smart Driver system as a way for parents to monitor teen drivers or for adults to track their driving behavior. But in 2024, it emerged that GM had been sharing that data with brokers. Those brokers then sold the data to insurance companies, and some drivers found that their insurance became more expensive as a result. To make matters worse, many of those drivers claimed they had no knowledge of ever agreeing to share such data for such purposes.

Last year, GM and its OnStar subsidiary entered into a settlement with the FTC, prohibiting them from sharing some kinds of driver data with third parties. The settlement was finalized this January. That agreement banned the two companies from sharing geolocation data or driver behavior data for five years. At the time, GM also discontinued Smart Driver across its entire range.
Now the automaker has reached terms with the District of Columbia and 35 states after their attorneys general joined together to sue GM as well.

GM told Reuters in a statement that “[s]afer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share.”

According to TechCrunch, the settlement with the states is notable in that it doesn’t take GM’s word that it’s complying with the privacy policy—a third party will be required to make that determination.

articles.headline: Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance
keyFacts: Blockchain intelligence firms TRM and Chainalysis attributed a $6.36 billion hack on cryptocurrency exchange Binance to North Korea's elite hacking unit, TraderTraitor.
Binance stated that it froze about $3 billion in affected assets, suspended withdrawals, and promised to cover all user losses.
Binance expects withdrawals to resume in the next day or two and is working with law enforcement to identify the criminals.
body: Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance
A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm says a North Korean unit was likely behind the hack that impacted more than $6 billion on Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets. It said Friday that it was beginning to recover assets for users.
The cryptocurrency exchange said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. It said it will cover all losses.
The company said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional "points of breach."
TRM, in a post on its website Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," the firm said.

"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.
In February last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.

Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was "likely done by DPRK group TraderTraitor," its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. DPRK stands for the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, North Korea's official name.

Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice."

Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.

In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.

Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform, and stepped down as the company's CEO. U.S. President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.

Zhao posted Thursday on X that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn't manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Binance said on X it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

articles.headline: Using AI to Vibe Code Your TV Is Stupid
keyFacts: Social media posts claim users can employ AI to code better, ad-free television operating systems with less tracking.
Experts warned that using AI to modify complex TV software risks breaking the device or creating security vulnerabilities.
The author stated that users can easily change Android TV interfaces with existing launcher apps instead of using AI.
body: Recently, some posts on X/Twitter and discussed elsewhere have claimed that AI has helped people “vibe code” their way to a better TV interface. Less clutter, no ads, less tracking and more are all ascribed to AI’s magical powers. Not only is this nonsense, but it’s also stupid.

First, let me say up front that I understand the frustration. TV interfaces have gotten bloated; they often have ads, and their creepy and invasive tracking properties have long been discussed and warned about by me and others.
That said, AI is not doing anything unique here. Not only can you do this without AI, but it’s also probably better if you don’t. Using AI risks potentially TV-ruining issues or worse.
More from CNET
What’s happening

“Vibe coding” is the colloquial term for using AI to assist or fully write programming code for apps, websites and so on. Instead of learning a programming language, people tell AI agents in plain English (or their language of choice) what they want, and the AI does it, or at least something close to it.
In this case, people are claiming they’re using an AI agent, usually Claude, to write a new operating system for TVs. This “new” OS is, they claim, faster, easier to use, has no ads and so on.
Why it’s a bad idea

As with all claims about AI, you should be suspicious. First, TV operating systems are far more complex than they appear. Messing around “under the hood,” especially with no programming knowledge, can easily cause serious problems.

One TV engineer I spoke to for this article, who asked to remain anonymous, literally laughed out loud when I asked him about this. He explained that his engineers will often fix one bug in their software, and it will cause 10 other bugs in random, seemingly unrelated parts of the TV. That’s pretty typical with software development, by the way. There are reports already that people have “bricked” their TVs trying this. As in, they turned their TV into an expensive and unusable brick.

There are also a lot of potential issues down the road, even if you have initial success. For instance, will the new vibe-coded OS actually run Netflix and other apps? They might seem to load and then not be able to play anything. What happens if one of the apps needs an update? Will you still be able to? What if that update requires a specific Android version? Maybe you won’t have any issues, but there’s no guarantee of that, and if you don’t have any background in software or coding, can you be sure that more AI vibe coding will fix the issue? Will you be able to perform a factory reset and restore it to the way it was when you bought it? Hopefully yes, but not necessarily.

If you’re not a programmer, how sure are you that the code you’re using is secure? How sure are you that it’s only doing what you want and not exposing your TV to external access? This isn’t as likely as just breaking your TV, but if you don’t know or understand what’s going on “under the hood,” can you really be sure?

And what’s the end goal here? If it’s a faster interface with fewer ads, you can do that already without AI, as I’ll discuss in the next section. If it’s to minimize tracking, maybe changing the OS or interface will help, but not entirely.
Why it’s really stupid: An easier solution already exists

AI can’t invent anything, and you can already change your TV’s interface with just an app install. Android TV launchers, as in the user interface, can be swapped out. So if your TV runs on Android, you can change the interface without any AI vibe coding. These launchers are often far simpler than the stock Google TV interface and are highly customizable.

Launchers like Projectivity, Monet and TV Launcher Premium Smart UI are some of the top-rated and most popular ones. The AT4K Launcher even makes your Android TV interface look like the Apple TV interface. There are many more options.

If you have a TV with a company-specific operating system, like LG’s webOS, Samsung’s Tizen, Hisense’s VIDAA and so on, the AI vibe coding trick isn’t likely to work anyway. Companies do their best to lock down their operating systems to prevent exactly the kind of thing we’re talking about here.
It’s entirely arguable that AI wasn’t doing anything clever in the first place. It was just regurgitating what human programmers had already figured out.
What you can do instead

I think there’s a hilarious irony in not wanting your personal data to be out there, so in order to block your TV from tracking you, you give your personal data to AI. If you don’t understand why that’s ironic, you definitely shouldn’t give your data to AI. As I’ve talked about before, there is no easy way to prevent your TV from tracking you and selling your data. You can minimize it, or go to more extreme measures like Pi-holes and not connecting it to the internet at all, but then you’ll just be switching which device is tracking you. Still want streaming? All the streaming devices track you to some extent (the Apple TV 4K less so).

Using AI to vibe code your way into a better TV experience, however, is a dumb idea. Try a launcher app first and see if that gets you most or all the way to what you’re looking for. Will it be a magical fix to speed up a slow TV? No, but it could be much closer to what you’re looking for, and it’s far less likely to nuke your TV. If you want to go even further, there are apps that give you even more control, but with more potential for issues. Or hey, if you have a TV you don’t mind ruining, and you want to see what you can come up with using an AI that is just stealing from other people’s work, go for it.
